title: The surgical treatment of idiopathic abnormal uterine bleeding: An analysis of 88 000 patients from the French exhaustive national hospital discharge database from 2009 to 2015
article_subtype: Retrospective study using a national hospital discharge database
condition_or_topic: Surgical treatment of idiopathic abnormal uterine bleeding (AUB)
clinical_background: AUB can substantially impair quality of life and may be classified as idiopathic when no underlying cause is identified. The choice of treatment depends on symptom severity and whether fertility preservation is desired. Medical and surgical options are available. The guidelines described in the article favour pharmacological treatment initially and identify second-generation endometrial ablation as a preferred surgical option when appropriate; first-generation techniques may be used if necessary, whereas first-line hysterectomy is not recommended in this setting. Systematic reviews and meta-analyses cited by the authors suggest that second-generation procedures have similar effectiveness to first-generation procedures with fewer complications.
objectives: Describe how the use of second-generation procedures, first-generation procedures, curettage and hysterectomy for idiopathic AUB changed over time.
Compare the success rates, severe complications and management costs of these four surgical approaches.
clinical_question: Among women aged between 35 and 55 years undergoing surgery for idiopathic AUB in France, how do second-generation procedures compare with first-generation procedures, curettage and hysterectomy in treatment success, severe complications and management costs?
interpretation: Among 109,884 women aged 35–55 years who underwent surgery for uncomplicated idiopathic AUB between 2009 and 2015, surgical practice did not align with French guidelines. Curettage and hysterectomy together accounted for more than half of procedures, while recommended 2G procedures represented no more than ten percent. Curettage had the highest failure rate; hysterectomy had the lowest failure rate but the highest severe-complication rate and cost. The number of women undergoing surgery fell by 13% between 2009 and 2015, chiefly alongside a 37% decline in curettage. Growth in 2G procedures did not offset that decline. The authors consider a shift toward nonsurgical care an insufficient explanation for the overall decrease because sales of IUD in France also fell during that period. They suggest that reimbursement differences may contribute to the limited use of 2G procedures, but their study did not examine why particular operations were chosen.
comparison_with_prior_evidence: French, English and Welsh, and Netherlands guidelines favor 2G procedures as the surgical option for idiopathic AUB when pharmacological treatment is ineffective; the Netherlands guidelines specifically favor radiofrequency ablation. The authors state that prior systematic reviews and meta-analyses support advantages of these procedures over hysterectomy or 1G procedures. The severe-complication rates observed after hysterectomy are consistent with recently published findings. By comparison, 2G procedures accounted for around one-third of surgery for idiopathic AUB in England in 2005. The authors also note prior evidence that failure after ablative procedures increases with time since treatment. According to the guidelines they cite, curettage is no longer recommended in any context in the 2013 Netherlands and 2018 Anglo-Welsh guidance.
clinical_implications: The observed outcomes suggest that 2G procedures have fewer severe complications and lower costs than hysterectomy, and greater treatment success than curettage or 1G procedures.
The authors consider 1G and 2G procedures potentially the most cost-effective strategies, while stressing that this was not a formal cost-effectiveness analysis.
Replacing curettage with 2G procedures could improve patient outcomes at little incremental cost; replacing hysterectomy with 2G procedures could yield substantial cost savings.
practice_implications: The authors highlight the gap between current surgical practice and guidelines that prefer 2G procedures for women with idiopathic AUB who have not responded to pharmacological treatment.
They state that switching to 2G procedures would not require surgeons to undertake specific training.
They suggest that higher DRG tariffs for 2G procedures could encourage their use.
limitations: The database does not document why a particular surgical procedure was selected, complicating attribution of complications to surgery.
Histological findings from surgical specimens were unavailable, so idiopathic AUB could not be verified through histology.
Because the database begins in 2006, some women operated on earlier may have been incorrectly classified as incident cases.
The database records hospital care but not community care, potentially underestimating actual costs and preventing a complete treatment history.

Age was used as a surrogate for fertility intentions. Some women over 35 who wished to preserve fertility may have been included, potentially increasing the observed number of curettages, while younger women who did not wish to have children were excluded.
The surgical pattern may differ in younger women or in women whose AUB has another cause, such as leiomyoma.
Differing tariffs may have led some 2G procedures to be coded as 1G procedures to obtain more favorable reimbursement.
Outcomes were not stratified by age to assess failure over time after the procedure. The authors expect any resulting bias to be minimal given the restricted age range.
strengths: The authors describe this as the largest reported cohort of patients surgically treated for idiopathic AUB.
The exhaustive national database enabled comprehensive capture of hospital surgery and follow-up; its large sample allowed precise outcome estimates.
The authors expect minimal bias from sampling error or loss to follow-up and consider coding errors uncommon.
open_questions: Why curettage remains widely used in France despite the cited guidance, and what prevents its replacement by more effective procedures.

Why some women were classified as treatment failures after hysterectomy: the authors suggest coding errors as a possibility and state that sub-total hysterectomies account for only 7% of these 3% failures.
future_directions: Investigate the continued use of curettage in France and barriers to replacing it with more effective surgery.
Compare the clinical and economic consequences of current idiopathic AUB surgical practice in observational clinical studies in France and other countries where practice may diverge from guidelines.
study_design: Retrospective study of the French national hospital discharge database Programme de Médicalisation des Systèmes d’Information (PMSI). Investigators identified women hospitalised for surgery for idiopathic abnormal uterine bleeding from 2009 to 2015 and compared outcomes across four procedure groups. Direct hospital costs were assessed from the perspective of the French social security system using national tariffs.

population.description: Women aged between 35 and 55 years who underwent hospital-based surgery for idiopathic abnormal uterine bleeding in France. The analysis included 109,884 women.
inclusion_criteria: A hospital stay between 1st January 2009 and 31st December 2015 with at least one CCAM code for abnormal uterine bleeding surgery and at least one ICD-10 code for idiopathic abnormal uterine bleeding recorded as a principal or related diagnosis in the medical unit where surgery was coded.
exclusion_criteria: Previous surgery for abnormal uterine bleeding identified through retrospective linkage until 2006.
Breast or colorectal cancer at or before inclusion, or von Willebrand disease at or before inclusion or during follow-up.
A hospital stay combining several idiopathic abnormal uterine bleeding procedures when assignment to one surgical group was not possible.

Concomitant conditions that could cause bleeding: myoma, gynaecological cancers, alcoholic liver disease, gynaecological or pelvic infection or inflammation, endometriosis, uro-gynaecological prolapse, fistulas, polyps or dysplasia, infertility, pregnancy, spina bifida, or blood diseases.
Artificial insemination attempts after curettage among patients aged 35–45 years.
population.care_setting: Overnight and day hospitalisations in public and private hospitals in France.

interventions: First generation (1G) endometrial ablation or resection, including loop resection or roller ball.
Second generation (2G) endometrial ablation, including radiofrequency ablation or balloon thermodestruction.
comparators: 2G procedures served as the reference for comparisons with 1G procedures, curettage and hysterectomy.

primary: Treatment failure, defined by another surgical intervention for abnormal uterine bleeding, persistent idiopathic abnormal uterine bleeding requiring hospital-based medical management, or pregnancy.

Severe complications linked to surgery and requiring hospitalisation; only events without an intervening surgical or interventional procedure were retained as certainly related to the abnormal uterine bleeding surgery.
secondary: Per capita direct hospital management costs at 18 months after surgery.
Use of each surgical procedure and distribution between overnight and day hospitalisation.

statistical_methods: Categorical variables were reported as proportions and assessed with the χ2 test or Fisher exact test. Continuous-variable mean differences were assessed with Student’s t-test. Kaplan-Meier curves tracked treatment failure and complications; rates for 1G procedures, curettage and hysterectomy were compared with 2G procedures using the Mantel-Cox log-rank test in unadjusted univariate analyses. Statistical significance was set at P values of < .05. Analyses used R statistical software (version 3.2.3). Hospital costs were assigned using French national tariffs and expressed in 2017 Euros.
follow_up: Patients operated on before mid-2014 were followed for at least 18 months and for up to 5 years if included in 2009 and 2010. Outcomes and complications were assessed at 18, 24 and 60 months; observation ended by 31st December 2015 or at death, with complication tracking also ending at treatment failure.

main_findings.context: 60 months; HR reported for Curettage versus 2G Surgery.

notable_adverse_events: At 18 months, severe complications occurred after 2G Surgery in 108 (1.9%) of N = 5 731, after 1G Surgery in 480 (1.5%) of N = 31 476, after Curettage in 452 (1.4%) of N = 32 307, and after Hysterectomy in 995 (5.3%) of N = 18 651.

At 24 months, severe complications occurred after 2G Surgery in 110 (2.2%) of N = 5 009, after 1G Surgery in 509 (1.8%) of N = 28 240, after Curettage in 469 (1.6%) of N = 29 833, and after Hysterectomy in 981 (5.8%) of N = 16 972.

At 60 months, severe complications occurred after 2G Surgery in 77 (4.6%) of N = 1 682, after 1G Surgery in 304 (2.7%) of N = 11 130, after Curettage in 353 (2.6%) of N = 13 417, and after Hysterectomy in 555 (7.9%) of N = 7 022.

Compared with 2G Surgery, Hysterectomy was associated with a significantly higher risk of severe complications at 18 months (HR 2.89; p<0.0001), 24 months (HR: 2.69; p<0.0001) and 60 months (HR: 1.77; p<0.0001).
The main complications reported after Hysterectomy were urogenital or abdominopelvic pain, infections, and surgical complications; rates for these individual complications were not provided.

secondary_results: Of 152,531 women aged 35–55 years identified between 1st January 2009 and 31st December 2015, 42,647 met an exclusion criterion and 109,884 remained for analysis. Follow-up was available for 88,165 at 18 months, 80,054 at 24 months and 33,251 at 60 months.
The mean participant age was 46 years, with no reported difference between surgery types.
In the analysis population, 7,863 women underwent 2G Surgery (7.2%), 39,935 underwent 1G Surgery (36.3%), 38,923 underwent Curettage (35.4%) and 23,163 underwent Hysterectomy (21.1%).

The number of women undergoing surgery fell by 13% between 2009 and 2015. Over that period, the number undergoing Curettage changed by -37%, Hysterectomy by -15%, 2G Surgery by +80% and 1G Surgery by +5%.

Nearly all Hysterectomy procedures involved an overnight stay, whereas most other procedures (around 80%) took place during day hospitalisation. The share of all procedures performed during day hospitalisation increased somewhat from 2009 to 2015.
For 2G Surgery, total per-patient hospitalisation costs at 18 months were a mean of € 2 448 ± 8 254, a median of € 1 173 [638–489 846] and an IQR of € 1 002–2 231; N = 5 730.
For 1G Surgery, total per-patient hospitalisation costs at 18 months were a mean of € 2 100 ± 3 476, a median of € 1 059 [529–157 965] and an IQR of € 913–2 075; N = 31 473.
For Curettage, total per-patient hospitalisation costs at 18 months were a mean of € 2 275 ± 5 278, a median of € 782 [244–424 261] and an IQR of € 741 - € 2 732; N = 32 304.
For Hysterectomy, total per-patient hospitalisation costs at 18 months were a mean of € 4 157 ± 3 535, a median of € 3 090 [1 129–112 002] and an IQR of € 2 909 - € 4 189; N = 18 647.
Both mean and median costs were highest after Hysterectomy and were described as almost two-fold higher than those of the other procedures at all assessed time points.

At 18 months, curettage had the highest failure proportion, while hysterectomy had the highest complication proportion.

main_conclusion: Surgical practice for idiopathic abnormal uterine bleeding did not align with the guidelines discussed by the authors: recommended 2G procedures were used in only ten percent of cases. Curettage had the highest failure rate, whereas hysterectomy had the lowest failure rate but the highest severe-complication rate and cost. The authors call for observational research comparing the clinical and economic consequences of current practice.
narrative_summary: This retrospective study used the exhaustive French hospital discharge database to compare surgical treatment of idiopathic abnormal uterine bleeding from 2009 to 2015. It included 109,884 women aged 35–55 years; 88,165 could be followed for 18 months. The procedures were 2G surgery in 7,863 women (7.2%), 1G surgery in 39,935 (36.3%), curettage in 38,923 (35.4%), and hysterectomy in 23,163 (21.1%). At 18 months, failure occurred in 9.9% after 2G surgery, 12.7% after 1G surgery, 20.6% after curettage and 2.8% after hysterectomy. Severe-complication rates at the same time were 1.9%, 1.5%, 1.4% and 5.3%, respectively. Median 18-month costs were € 1 173, € 1 059, € 782 and € 3 090, respectively. Compared with 2G surgery, 1G surgery and curettage had significantly greater risks of failure at 18 months (HR: 1.30 and HR: 2.21, respectively; p<0.0001); hysterectomy had a significantly greater risk of severe complications (HR 2.89; p<0.0001). The authors conclude that curettage and hysterectomy remained common despite the clinical and cost outcomes observed, while guideline-preferred 2G procedures were infrequently used. They note that the database lacked information on why procedures were chosen and on care delivered outside hospitals.

document_sections.heading: Objective
document_sections.content: The study aimed to compare treatment success, complications and management costs across surgical approaches to abnormal uterine bleeding (AUB).

document_sections.heading: Methods
document_sections.content: The authors retrospectively examined the French national hospital discharge database. They identified hospital stays from 2009 through 2015 that had both an AUB diagnosis code and a relevant surgical procedure code, yielding 109,884 women. Outcomes were compared across second-generation procedures (2G surgery), first-generation procedures (1G surgery), curettage and hysterectomy. Follow-up outcomes comprised treatment failure and complications; costs were assigned using standard French hospital tariffs.

document_sections.heading: Results
document_sections.content: Of the women studied, 7,863 received a 2G procedure (7.2%), 39,935 a 1G procedure (36.3%), 38,923 curettage (35.4%) and 23,163 hysterectomy (21.1%). At 18 months, failure rates were 9.9% after 2G surgery, 12.7% after 1G surgery, 20.6% after curettage and 2.8% after hysterectomy. Corresponding complication rates at 18 months were 1.9%, 1.5%, 1.4% and 5.3%. Median costs over 18 months were € 1 173, € 1 059, € 782 and € 3 090, respectively.

document_sections.heading: Conclusion
document_sections.content: Curettage had the greatest failure rate. Hysterectomy had the lowest failure rate, but also the greatest complication rate and cost. Despite favorable clinical outcomes and comparatively low costs, 1G and 2G procedures were used infrequently. The authors conclude that practice does not follow current AUB guidance: recommended 2G procedures were performed in <10% of cases.

document_sections.heading: Introduction
document_sections.content: AUB is defined by at least one of three features: menstruation lasting more than seven days, menstrual blood loss greater than 80 ml, or a PBAC (pictorial menstrual blood loss assessment chart) score 100. An estimated twenty to thirty percent of women of reproductive age experience AUB at some point. A population survey across five European countries found that 27.2% reported two or more AUB symptoms during the preceding year. Prevalence rises with age until menopause. AUB can result from an underlying condition, often leiomyoma, malignancy or a coagulopathy; when no cause is found, it is regarded as idiopathic. AUB significantly worsens health-related quality of life. In the European survey, over half of respondents with AUB described a major or moderate adverse effect on sexual life, physical activity and work productivity. Their Short-Form 36 Health Survey scores fell below the 25th percentile of national norms. A Finland study from 2001 reported that 20% of women with objectively documented AUB had missed work because of it during the previous six months. Treating idiopathic AUB can relieve symptoms and improve quality of life. Treatment selection depends on symptom severity and whether fertility preservation is desired. Medical options include oral contraceptives containing oestrogen plus progestin or progestin alone, tranexamic acid, mefenamic acid, gonadotropin-releasing hormone analogues and intrauterine systems (IUS) containing lævonorgestrel. Surgical options include curettage, hysterectomy and first-generation hysteroscopic approaches such as resection, roller-ball and laser ablation. Second-generation approaches include thermal balloon, cryoablation, microwave ablation and radiofrequency ablation. Cited systematic reviews and meta-analyses suggest that second-generation endometrial ablation appears similarly effective to first-generation treatment, with fewer complications; it may more often permit local anaesthesia or cervical block and require less operating time. Those reviews considered second-generation treatment more cost-effective despite higher observed rates of equipment failure and inability to finish the procedure. French guidelines and guidance from the Netherlands, England and Wales, the USA and Canada place pharmacological treatment first for idiopathic AUB as defined by the COEIN classification. For women with idiopathic AUB who do not want a future pregnancy, conservative surgery has greater long-term efficacy than oral medication and should be offered when tranexamic acid or a lævonorgestrel-containing IUS has insufficient effect. The guidelines favor second-generation endometrial ablation, with first-generation techniques used if necessary; they do not recommend hysterectomy as an initial treatment in this setting. They describe the effectiveness of curettage as unpredictable and temporary and restrict its acceptability in relation to fertility preservation. The study sought to describe changes in the use of four approaches—second-generation procedures, curettage, first-generation procedures and hysterectomy—and compare their success, severe complications and management costs.

document_sections.heading: Materials and methods Ethics
document_sections.content: The study followed applicable international and French regulatory requirements. Ethics committee approval was not required because the analysis used an anonymised database retrospectively and did not affect patient care. The French national data protection agency, CNIL, had approved use of PMSI-MCO for this type of research under annual authorisation #1419102 v7–2015-111111-56-18 / order M14N056 and M14L056.

document_sections.heading: Study design
document_sections.content: This retrospective study used the French Hospital medical information database, Programme de Médicalisation des Systèmes d’Information (PMSI). Its population comprised patients hospitalised in France for surgery to treat idiopathic AUB from 2009 to 2015. Data extraction and analysis followed French Health Ministry guidance on use of PMSI.

document_sections.heading: PMSI database
document_sections.content: PMSI-MCO (Médecine, Chirurgie, Obstétrique) is an exhaustive administrative and medical discharge database covering overnight and day admissions for short-term medical, surgical and obstetric care in French public and private hospitals. French health authorities use it to administer hospital funding. Each year it records almost 30 million stays involving over 13 million patients; it covers all public and private hospitals without sampling. Physicians identify reasons for admission with International Classification of Diseases, 10th revision (ICD-10) codes. These may designate the principal diagnosis (PD), a related underlying diagnosis (RD), or a significantly-associated diagnosis (SAD) representing a comorbidity or complication that could affect the admission or its cost. Stays are assigned diagnosis-related groups (DRG), and procedures are classified using the French Classification of Medical Procedures (CCAM, Classification Commune des Actes Médicaux).

document_sections.heading: Study population
document_sections.content: The authors identified French hospital stays between 1st January 2009 and 31st December 2015 with at least one CCAM code for AUB surgery and at least one ICD-10 code for idiopathic AUB recorded as a PD or RD in the unit coding the surgery. The codes, listed in S2 Table and S3 Table, excluded post-menopausal bleeding. Eligibility was restricted to women aged between 35 and 55 years. The lower limit of 35 years served as a proxy to exclude most women wishing to preserve fertility, a preference not recorded in the database, because all assessed procedures except curettage are indicated only when further childbearing is not desired. Each stay was assigned to one of four categories: first-generation (1G) endometrial ablation or resection, including loop resection or roller ball; second-generation (2G) ablation, including radiofrequency ablation or balloon thermodestruction; hysterectomy; or curettage. To retain incident cases, prior AUB surgery was sought retrospectively through 2006 and affected patients were excluded. An algorithm developed with the scientific committee also excluded patients with potentially biasing conditions or circumstances: breast or colorectal cancer at or before inclusion, traced back to 2006; von Willebrand disease at or before inclusion, traced back to 2006, or during follow-up through end 2015; stays containing more than one idiopathic AUB operation and thus not assignable to a single group; conditions that could themselves cause bleeding, including myoma, gynaecological cancers, alcoholic liver disease, gynaecological or pelvic infection and inflammation, endometriosis, uro-gynaecological prolapse, fistulas, polyps and dysplasia, infertility, pregnancy, spina bifida and blood diseases; and artificial insemination attempts after curettage among patients aged 35–45 years. Women operated on before mid-2014 had at least 18 months of follow-up, extending up to 5 years for those included in 2009 and 2010. Outcomes were assessed from surgery until 31st December 2015, or earlier death. Success required absence of all failure criteria: another AUB operation (1G, 2G, curettage or hysterectomy), persistent idiopathic AUB requiring hospital medical management, and pregnancy. Severe complications were surgery-linked medical events requiring hospitalisation. They were tracked until 31st December 2015, death or treatment failure. Inflammatory disorders, haemoperitoneum and systemic complications—anaemia, shock, a complication directly linked to surgery, pain, infection or a blood-supply disorder—were considered acute when they occurred within 30 days. Other complications in the urogenital, abdominal or pelvic region could occur at any subsequent time; examples included adhesions, foreign body, pain, ventral hernia, renal failure, intestinal obstruction, other digestive disorders, and urological or genital disorders. Complications were identified with ICD10 codes. Because another operation or intervention could have caused a subsequent event, the analysis retained only complications without an intervening procedure as certainly attributable to AUB surgery.

document_sections.heading: Data collection
document_sections.content: Age was recorded at inclusion. For each initial admission, the authors assessed whether care involved an overnight stay or day hospitalisation. Among women operated on before mid-2014, they documented outcomes and complication rates at 18, 24 and 60 months. They also recorded total hospital resource use across admissions from the index admission through any admission for failure or complication. Outpatient-prescribed or outpatient-dispensed medicines were not included because the database did not capture them.

document_sections.heading: Costing
document_sections.content: Per-patient costs at 18 months after idiopathic AUB surgery were estimated for each cohort. The analysis included direct costs from the perspective of the French social security system, National Health Insurance (NHI). Official French tariffs for medical acts applicable from 2009 to 2015 were used, with amounts expressed in 2017 Euros after Consumer Price Index adjustment. Each admission received the national tariff associated with its PMSI DRG. These tariffs covered medical and related procedures, nursing, treatments other than specified expensive medicines and implants, food, accommodation and hospital investment costs. Applicable intensive-care costs were added per hospital day. For private hospitals, physician fees identified through ENCC (Echelle Nationale des Coûts à méthodologie Commune) were added because physicians were reimbursed fee-for-service; public-hospital physician costs were already incorporated in DRG tariffs as personnel costs. Expensive medicines and implants were priced from the public FICHCOMP database or the official private-sector tariff. Because private-sector FICHCOMP data were unavailable for 2009, the 2009 costs of these items were assigned using mean FICHCOMP-derived public-hospital costs for 2009.

document_sections.heading: Statistical analysis
document_sections.content: Categorical variables were reported as proportions and assessed with the χ2 test or Fisher exact test. Univariate comparisons of continuous-variable means used Student’s t-test. Kaplan-Meier curves tracked treatment failure and complications over time. The authors compared each of the other three procedures against 2G procedures as the reference using the Mantel-Cox log-rank test in an unadjusted univariate analysis. Statistical significance was set at P values of < .05. Analyses used R version 3.2.3.

document_sections.heading: Results Study population
document_sections.content: From 1st January 2009 through 31st December 2015, PMSI identified 152,531 women aged 35–55 years who were hospitalised for idiopathic AUB surgery. Of these, 42,647 met at least one exclusion criterion, leaving 109,884 for analysis. Follow-up was available for 88,165 women at 18 months, 80,054 at 24 months and 33,251 at 60 months. Mean participant age was 46 years, without an age difference between procedure groups.

document_sections.heading: Surgery for idiopathic abnormal uterine bleeding
document_sections.content: Among the 109,884 women analysed, 7,863 underwent a 2G procedure (7.2%), 39,935 a 1G procedure (36.3%), 38,923 curettage (35.4%) and 23,163 hysterectomy (21.1%). The number undergoing surgery fell by 13% between 2009 and 2015. Curettage declined by -37% and hysterectomy by -15%, while 2G procedures rose by +80%; 1G procedure numbers were relatively stable at +5%. Almost every hysterectomy required an overnight admission, whereas most other procedures—around 80%—took place as day hospitalisations. The day-hospitalisation share across all procedures rose somewhat from 2009 to 2015.

document_sections.heading: Treatment outcome
document_sections.content: At 18 months, treatment failure ranged from 2.8% after hysterectomy to 20.6% after curettage. Compared with 2G procedures, failure risk at 18 months was significantly higher after 1G surgery (HR: 1.30; p<0.0001) and curettage (HR: 2.21; p<0.0001). Elevated risks were also reported at 24 months for 1G procedures (HR: 1.26; p<0.0001) and curettage (HR: 2.21; p<0.0001). At 60 months, a significantly elevated risk was reported for curettage only (HR 1.75; p<0.0001).

document_sections.heading: Table 1. Treatment failures and complications in women undergoing surgery for idiopathic abnormal uterine bleeding.
document_sections.content: The table gives the numbers of women evaluated and the counts and proportions with treatment failure or complications at 18 months, 24 months and 60 months for 2G Surgery, 1G Surgery, Curettage and Hysterectomy. Its note identifies statistically significant comparisons with 2G surgery using a Cox model (p<0.0001).

document_sections.heading: Table 2. Per capita total 18-month costs of management of women undergoing surgery for idiopathic abnormal uterine bleeding.
document_sections.content: The table presents cohort sizes and mean, median, range and interquartile-range per-patient management costs at 18 months for 2G Surgery, 1G Surgery, Curettage and Hysterectomy. Means are accompanied by standard deviations. Its note identifies statistically significant comparisons with 2G Surgery using a t-test (p<0.0001).

document_sections.heading: Severe complications
document_sections.content: At 18 months, severe complications ranged from 1.4% after curettage to 5.3% after hysterectomy. Relative to 2G procedures, hysterectomy was associated with significantly greater severe-complication risk at 18 months (HR 2.89; p<0.0001), 24 months (HR: 2.69; p<0.0001) and 60 months (HR: 1.77; p<0.0001). The main complications reported after hysterectomy were urogenital or abdominopelvic pain, infection and surgical complications.

document_sections.heading: Cost of hospitalisation
document_sections.content: Mean and median per-patient hospitalisation costs were highest after hysterectomy. At every assessed time point, they were almost two-fold greater than costs for the other procedure types.

document_sections.heading: Discussion
document_sections.content: The authors describe their cohort of 109,884 women aged between 35 and 55 years who underwent surgery for uncomplicated idiopathic AUB from 2009 to 2015 as the largest reported for this condition. They conclude that French practice diverged from national guidance: curettage and hysterectomy, neither recommended as a first-line surgical choice, together represented over half of operations, despite hysterectomy costing over twice as much as other procedures and curettage having a two-fold higher failure rate. Second-generation procedures were least used, accounting for no more than ten percent of operations. Surgery volume fell by 13% between 2009 and 2015, mainly because curettage fell by 37%. A concurrent doubling of 2G procedures did not offset that decrease. The authors note that IUD sales in France also fell during this period; accordingly, they argue that a move to non-surgical interventions cannot explain the decline in surgery. Use of PMSI provided exhaustive coverage of hospital surgery and follow-up, a large sample allowing precise outcome estimates, and expected minimal sampling and follow-up bias; the authors consider coding errors uncommon. Nevertheless, different tariffs could have prompted some 2G procedures to be coded as 1G to obtain better reimbursement. A major limitation is the absence of documented reasons for selecting a procedure, especially when assessing whether surgery caused a complication; the study was intended to describe procedures performed, not why they were selected. Histological findings were unavailable, preventing histological confirmation of idiopathic AUB. Because PMSI begins in 2006, some women operated on earlier could have been misclassified as incident cases. PMSI also omits community care, potentially understating actual costs and preventing a complete treatment history. Generalisability is limited to idiopathic AUB in women aged 35 – 55 years old. The lower age cutoff was intended to reduce inclusion of women wishing to preserve fertility, but age is an imperfect proxy: women over 35 who wanted children may have been included, inflating curettage use, while younger women who did not want children and received another studied procedure were excluded. Surgical patterns may differ among younger women, who have longer potential childbearing periods, or among women whose AUB has another cause such as leiomyoma. The authors consider AUB causes likely to differ between younger women and their study population. French, English and Welsh, and Netherlands guidance favors 2G surgery after inadequate response to pharmacological treatment; Netherlands guidance specifically recommends radiofrequency ablation. The authors attribute these recommendations to cited meta-analyses and systematic reviews reporting advantages over hysterectomy or 1G procedures. Their own results suggest lower severe-complication rates and costs for 2G procedures than for hysterectomy, and greater success than with curettage or 1G procedures. Although hysterectomy complication rates might appear high, the authors state that they agree with recently published findings. They contrast French use with England, where 2G procedures already accounted for around one-third of idiopathic AUB operations in 2005. They propose that lower reimbursement for 2G procedures might financially favor 1G surgery. Without claiming a formal cost-effectiveness analysis, they suggest that 1G and 2G approaches appear the most cost-effective. Curettage, 1G and 2G have similar costs; curettage has the greatest failure rate, while hysterectomy has the lowest failure rate but the greatest severe-complication rate and cost. They find the 3% hysterectomy failure rate unexpected: sub-total hysterectomies account for 7% of these 3% and cannot fully explain it, while coding errors could contribute. Cited research reports that failure after ablation rises with time since treatment. The authors did not stratify failure over time by age because their age range was limited; they expect little resulting bias. They observe that widespread curettage use is surprising because the 2010 French guidelines regard it as acceptable only when fertility preservation is needed. Fertility intentions were not available in PMSI, although the authors consider women aged 35–55 years less likely than younger women to wish to retain fertility. The 2013 Netherlands and 2018 Anglo-Welsh guidelines no longer recommend curettage in any setting. The authors call for research into why curettage remains common in France and what prevents its replacement with more effective operations. They state that changing to 2G procedures would not require specific surgeon training; replacing curettage could improve outcomes at little additional cost, and replacing hysterectomy could substantially reduce costs. They suggest that higher DRG tariffs for 2G procedures could encourage adoption.

document_sections.content: The article identifies supplementary tables covering age and hospitalisation in the study population, CCAM codes for AUB surgery, and ICD-10 codes for idiopathic AUB; their detailed contents are not provided here.
